265: Tita and La Cueva del Zoncho

Everyone who has been to La Cueva del Zoncho in Santa María de Dota knows this magical place is what it is thanks to an inspiring woman who decided to make La Cueva more than her home, turning it into a space filled with history, art, and culture built over three decades.

veryone who has been to La Cueva del Zoncho in Santa María de Dota knows this magical place is what it is thanks to an inspiring woman who decided to make La Cueva more than her home, turning it into a space filled with history, art, and culture that
has been built over three decades.

We are talking about Flor Emilia Ureña, better known as Tita, whom we drew away from her routine to chat and learn more about her life. Naturally, she welcomed us with a smile and a long, colorful dress, two of her trademarks.
Nearly 66 years ago, Tita was born in an adobe house in Santa María, as she explains when we ask about her childhood:

“I think my childhood was the most beautiful, and my life has been very lovely. We were free back then: no cell phones, no cars, no electricity. My childhood was very different from yours. I consider myself a happy person. Like anyone, things happen, you feel down and try to get back up, but I have lived very, very well in this town.”
Tita tells us that loquats, jocotes, lemons, and oranges are her favorite fruits because of the beautiful childhood memories they bring back. The pandemic allowed her to recreate those moments:

“During the pandemic, I said, ‘The business is closed, so I am going to do what I used to!’ I went to my siblings’ farms to pick mangoes and loquats, and every day I ate fruit like when I was little. I daydreamed and relived my childhood. That was how it was: you left home after some aguadulce and a piece of bread and went to play all over town, eating guavas, loquats, and jocotes.”

Tita says her parents taught her to work from the age of five. She is deeply grateful for that because it allowed her to build what she has today through hard work and enjoy unique experiences she never imagined, such as living in Panama for ten years.

“In Panama, after the invasion, I moved to one of the most troubled neighborhoods. I lived there and saw so much from my balcony that I also learned not to judge people, because I imagined what it would have been like to be born there, where women carried a knife behind their backs and children were made to sell drugs. I think those experiences helped me run this place, La Cueva.”

She has been in charge of La Cueva, her business and home, for 33 years, since her father died. She told us he built it between 1967 and 1969 from a very old adobe house, adding a room at the back to use as a dance hall.
“People had already called this place La Cueva, because a man nicknamed ‘Pata e’zoncho’ helped my dad build it. People came and said, ‘Look, this is the vulture’s cave!’ And the name stuck.”
But what, according to Tita, makes La Cueva so beloved by so many people and generations from Los Santos and beyond?

“Because I live here, my motto has always been that everyone is welcome in my home and should feel at home, knowing I am someone who will not judge anyone. Bohemians from around the world come here; everyone has a story and a life. The people who come here are intelligent. Some people have become angry because I want to make room for everyone, but I tell them this is how La Cueva is. If they want to come, they can, but I am not changing the rules.”
There are clearly defined rules at La Cueva, and they are strictly enforced. Some are:
Anyone can enter La Cueva.
Anyone who fights gets water thrown on them.
Anyone who sells drugs is banned from returning.
People who use drugs are not allowed to use them inside La Cueva.
“I believe every place has its charm and energy if you experience it with passion.”

Those of us who live in Los Santos see every summer how La Cueva welcomes hundreds of Indigenous and Nicaraguan people who come to work in the coffee harvest. But why has Tita opened her door to these communities, who often face rejection elsewhere?

“I always heard how Nicaraguan and Indigenous people were treated. I did not know much about their cultures, but I became very interested in learning. I asked them to take me traveling, and that is why I have made fourteen trips to Nicaragua, to many marginalized areas. People asked why I went to those neighborhoods if they were dangerous, but because I went with an energy of love, God always protects you. I learned so much about their culture there, and I love their food. They are very humble people; many live in remote rural areas, and they are not bad people. I think that if reincarnation exists, in a past life I was Nicaraguan or Indigenous.”

Tita’s many trips to Nicaragua are a small part of her travels across the 28 countries she has visited. She has returned to some more than once, including Guatemala, which she has visited thirteen times, and Panama, which she still visits frequently.
All these experiences emerge in conversation with Tita, making the value culture brings to people’s lives clear to anyone.
“When you get to know other cultures, you can consider what is right or wrong for each of them. It is better to visit each place, adapt, and show respect. That is what you learn most: respect.”

Tita has always been open to every form of cultural and artistic expression. That is why she has turned La Cueva into a nationally recognized stage that has welcomed hundreds of musicians over the years, even helping launch dozens of local bands that took their first steps there.

“I had seen rock bands at big fairs in other countries, and those beautiful concerts gave me goosebumps. What a beautiful thing! I would say, ‘How lovely if they came to La Cueva one day!’ But I did not have the space or capacity for groups like that. In those years, young people from town came to tell me they had instruments and music and wanted to put on a concert here. I said, ‘Of course, come!’ Sometimes I hid because it sounded awful and I felt embarrassed, but we had to encourage and support them. If someone ever objects to concerts in my business, fine, but I can die in peace because we have already broken down that idea of ‘singing to the devil.’ We are becoming more aware, because that came from a lack of education.”

Tita tells us it is very important to keep creating new places in the region and organizing artistic activities for children, young people, and adults, to encourage and educate the community through art. She assures us La Cueva will always be available to anyone wanting to make music, put on theater, hold reading circles, play board games, or organize any other activity. That is what La Cueva del Zoncho is for: going there and enjoying it.

For the Santos Rock Cultural Association, Tita’s energy and support have been vital to our collective’s development. She joins our activities, advises us, and always opens her doors to diverse cultural events and spaces. We believe Tita deserves every recognition from Los Santos for promoting local culture for decades. We hope more and more people make La Cueva their home and a place to meet, have fun, and gather, just as she has always wanted.
2457: A festival twenty years later: A personal history of Santos Rock

That afternoon we were in San Pablo when the police stopped us and took us to the station. Jonathan, Luis, and me. Jonathan and I had taken a local bus from Santa María. We stopped in San Marcos, where Luis joined us. I was carrying a jar of starch paste my mom had helped me make. Jonathan had a bag of printed festival posters.

That afternoon we were in San Pablo when the police stopped us and took us to the station. Jonathan, Luis, and me. Jonathan and I had taken a local bus from Santa María. We stopped in San Marcos, where Luis joined us. I was carrying a jar of starch paste my mom had helped me make. Jonathan had a bag of printed festival posters.

It was late in the year. This was the second Santos Rock festival. We were kids—I was about to turn seventeen—and there at the station, Jonathan and I had no idea what to do. Luis did: he asked for the phone and called a friend of his dad’s who was a lawyer. They let us go immediately.

I had learned something a year earlier. Putting on a festival almost alone, with no experience, is a very effective form of torture. Even so, a year later I wanted to do it again, though with less pain and frustration this time. From the outset, I knew it would be best to involve more people. Many friends had seen what happened in 2006 and joined in.

Nanú and I had pushed the first festival forward, with occasional help from other friends before and after the event. Nothing systematic. But what happened at that first edition sparked enthusiasm in many more people. It showed us that a music festival in those little Los Santos towns really had potential. We had to keep going. Even if we screwed up. Screwed up again. Screwed up better.
Akoska at Santos Rock 2006
A regional music scene

My cousin Mela had taken over as president of the Cantonal Young Persons Committee during that period. When she arrived, she found a surplus of unspent money. Although she already had some ideas about what to do with it, she asked me what else I could think of.

At the time, I was really into music magazines—especially the ones that reached Costa Rica from Spain at least six months late. Those magazines often reviewed Europe’s summer festivals. Lots of bands, sound and lights, people and beer. That combination of elements—and here is the key—came together outdoors, with sunshine and mountains.

Meanwhile, the first Costa Rock had taken place in late 2006, organized by Giovanny Durán of El Guato. The festival brought together thirty-three Costa Rican pop, rock, metal, punk, ska, and reggae bands in an event that started at noon and ended at midnight. Although I was a fifteen-year-old kid, I managed to pass my enthusiasm on to a responsible adult—meaning my older brother, René.

René had the idea of renting a minibus for about ten people, buying ten festival tickets, and advertising a package with admission and round-trip travel from Los Santos. That was how I started pasting posters on utility poles. We gathered ten people and headed to Paraíso de Cartago at the end of October.

For a kid like me, drinking in “Costa Rican rock” from the inexhaustible source that was Radio U—especially shows such as Punto de Garaje—going to that festival was a revelation. I saw many bands I loved; the Hormigas en la Pared performance is burned into my memory. Many of us also discovered bands just starting to become known, such as Los Cuchillos, who had appeared on the scene a year earlier.
Part of the Los Santos contingent at Costa Rock (2007)

With that recent Costa Rock experience in mind, alongside the collection of magazines piling up in my room, full of photographs of festivals surrounded by mountains, I had an idea that I shared with Melania. I probably said something like: “Mela, what if we used the committee’s money to put on a music festival at El Guayabal?”

El Guayabal was already well known in the region. It hosted interschool dances. In the pasture and small wood surrounding the hall, plenty of people had their first kisses and received a few anatomy lessons. At the time, it also still hosted livestock fairs, which drew far more than cattle experts: people from all three Los Santos cantons came for the dances, ranchera and tropical music concerts, saturated fats, and alcohol.

I knew immediately that the place was perfect for a music festival. We certainly never aspired to draw the crowds that attended the livestock fairs, but we could trust that a good number of people would come. Especially because, thanks to the Young Persons Committee’s funding, the first festival was free. Above all, though, what we wanted to highlight—or the festival’s goal, really—was that it could be sustained mainly by local bands from the three Los Santos cantons and neighboring towns in southern San José and Cartago. These local bands would also share the stage with bands from the “national scene” that we liked and admired.
A year earlier—in 2005—I had attended a concert at La Cueva.
Rock of Tarrazú

read the poster I came across one afternoon on my way home from school. Seeing that poster, printed on red paper, was how I first learned that the neighboring canton had a music scene. [For the record: that show was when I discovered the Tarrazú scene, but it had already been active for many years.]

The concert would be at La Cueva in Santa María de Dota, just a few meters from home. I did what I needed to get my mom’s permission and went. Manrique Sánchez must have organized it; he was very active in several music projects and in organizing shows at the time. I do not remember exactly which bands played. I do remember Sobredosis, one of my favorite Los Santos bands. Punto de Partida and Pandemia—Manrique’s project back then—probably played too, and perhaps one of the many bands Pablo Zúñiga has put together. I think he was flirting with black metal and goth at the time and had formed a band called Sontuniversia.
That fortunate convergence let us move from idea to action. I was discovering that music festivals were important events in Costa Rica’s music scene. I could see that our town had suitable
spots

for putting one together. At the same time, I could see a music scene forming that was already moving beyond the cantons’ narrow geographical limits and the historic—and stupid—rivalries that made otherwise weak, insignificant borders seem so pronounced.

Back then, a thrash metal band called Equinoxis had formed at Dota’s high school. Its members came from Santa María and San Gerardo de Dota. Little by little, they also started getting together with bands from San Marcos. Rock was no longer music made only in Tarrazú. A regional scene was taking shape.
Equinoxis, Gargamel, Punto de Partida, and Backdraft at Cine Yirá (2007)
It is 2006, and the noise reaches El Guayabal

It must have been one of those Saturdays when Andrés and Michi, two musician friends from San Martín de León Cortés, would visit me to exchange music. I told them about the festival idea. At some point I also brought it to Nanú. Although I first put the idea into words with Michi and Andrés, it was with Nanú that the project got moving.

It may sound like a cliché. Stories are full of those pairings: Holmes and Watson, Batman and Robin, Pinky and the Brain. They all combine the same things. One embodies visionary madness, unrestrained impulse, imagination that overflows the bounds of good sense. The other contributes practical will and feet on the ground. While one invents the world, the other lives in it. That is what my friendship with Nanú has been like, and how I would describe the birth of Santos Rock. Madness needs willpower so it does not evaporate into pure fantasy, and willpower needs madness so it does not rot into mere routine.

People who know Nanú might say he embodies the madness in that equation, but at first it was the other way around. Nanú is about four years older than me. At the time, I was a timid, frightened minor. Nanú, meanwhile, had daring: he already had a license, drove “el Pichirilo”—his grandfather’s car—and possessed a wealth of practical knowledge that I, an inhabitant of my room’s bookish fantasy world, lacked. He took ownership of the idea and tackled many essential tasks that I could not or did not dare to undertake.
Left to right: Jesús, Nanú, and Jonathan, with el Pichirilo behind them (2007)

With Nanú as my partner and many other friends supporting us, things began moving. With Melania’s backing, we presented the project to the Cantonal Young Persons Committee, and our budget was approved. Having that money was a relief, and I still think it was more than that: it was a push forward, a way to see that the idea was possible. Being able to hire professional sound and cover many logistical expenses made us feel more secure. We began with greater confidence, putting together a call for bands, designing a poster in the most amateur way, and covering utility poles with starch paste.

That does not mean everything was simple. Again, we were teenagers with zero experience. Taking on tasks as we went, for which we were clearly unqualified, was a challenge. Picture that teenager shut in his room, trying to negotiate with a sound engineer who mentioned things called a “
rider
” or a “
backline
.” Those concepts were new and completely unfamiliar to me. I had to ask and learn.

Perhaps most importantly, many of our musician friends learned too. Once on the festival stage—or rather, the truck trailer serving as a stage—they discovered that stage monitors existed. These let them hear what they were playing instead of being drowned in noise and amplifier feedback. They learned to ask for “more gain” on their instruments, to use that equipment, and to try to sound better. Our learning was shared and collective.
Pandemia and the famous truck stage (2007)
But if navigating the preparations and reaching festival day in decent shape was difficult, the day itself revealed things we had not anticipated. The event had barely started when we discovered
on the spot

many other problems. Neither the bands nor we as organizers knew how to enforce a schedule or manage smooth transitions between performance times, running order, and downtime—while one band left the stage and another came on, soundchecked, and began playing. Many bands never arrived. Others arrived late. The closing band decided to play earlier so they could watch the national football match. It was a disastrous recipe for upsetting many musicians—with good reason—and sending me into crisis.
Again, we had to learn, take the knocks, and realize that this unwritten manual was really a living notebook of experiences.

“We could quickly become frustrated, put our ambitions and projects away in a drawer, and each go our own way. Or we could pay attention to those experiences and do something with them, so we could continue with a better understanding of what we were doing.”
2007, a new edition: No money, but (
some
) experience

After seeing what was possible in 2006, we put together the second Santos Rock in December 2007. We no longer had funding, but we had learned something from the first festival. We decided we could manage it ourselves by holding a series of small concerts in local bars throughout the year, gradually raising money to finance the bigger event at year’s end.

There was Nanú, driving el Pichirilo everywhere, hauling Tito Zafiro’s amplifiers and drum kit. Friends and bands took part in those smaller events with a clear understanding: nobody kept the door money; it all went into a fund to be used entirely for Santos Rock. We called the concept “sábado acusticazo.” It generally used a smaller format with fewer technical requirements. The invitation and the formula worked, although the money was not enough.
Sábado acusticazo at La Cueva (2007)

When festival day arrived at the end of the year, some of us contributed from our thin student wallets and recovered the money at later concerts. What mattered was seeing that the project could exist without support from institutions or potential sponsors. Two things played important roles: first, the many more people who joined after seeing what happened in 2006; second, the availability of places tolerant of noise and lively young people passionate about music.
Talking about how this music scene developed in Los Santos means recognizing and thanking the willingness and support of people such as
Tita and her daughter Xóchitl at “La Cueva

and Tita’s brother, Jose Ureña, at El Guayabal. La Cueva bar in Santa María de Dota, and Tita’s openness to letting ska, punk, and even the most extreme metal bands make noise there, allowed this music scene to emerge, endure, and transform. Holding a festival like Santos Rock in 2007—again, without sponsors or any public or private institutional backing—was only possible because Tita and La Cueva were always willing to host the smaller concerts that financed the bigger event.
In fact, any music scene’s dependence on its venues explains why the festival reached an
impasse

after that second edition in 2007. The day before the event, many Santa María residents heard the priest’s sermon at Mass. He warned how inappropriate it was for that small town to give free rein to libertine, sinful activities such as a rock festival. The sermon worked. Our impression was that more people attended than the previous year. But the voices of disapproval, backed by the priest’s words, meant we lost the opportunity to repeat the festival at El Guayabal. Although we tried to find a new venue elsewhere in Los Santos, the search failed, and many of us became discouraged.
After a Sábado Acusticazo at La Cueva. Left to right: Tito, Jesús, and Nanú. Below: Jonathan
Ten years without Santos Rock (
but with plenty happening

In 2008, I was in eleventh grade. Although I kept looking for places to organize concerts and stay close to friends making music, things began changing for me and many of my friends. Some of us soon moved to San José and started university, while others began working. We only traveled back occasionally, and many of those new projects interrupted our musical ambitions.

That does not mean the Los Santos music scene died in those years. Many younger friends also started music projects, secured venues, created their own festivals, and undertook truly admirable efforts. That was how I met Gabo Montero, who began organizing metal shows and later joined Pablo Zúñiga in Istanbul, a project that brought sounds not very common in Los Santos at the time. The extreme metal scene was also very active, with bands such as Scars of Destruction, Suicidal Brain, and Dead Ivory. The latter included Andrey Araya, “Cabecita,” who had also belonged to the earlier generation from the early 2000s. Like Manrique Sánchez, Alejandro Vega “Tito,” Douglas Picado, and many others, he joined people starting bands in the early 2010s.

Alongside concerts at private parties, members of that incoming generation, such as Alex Jiménez and Edgar Muñoz with their Suicidal Brain bandmates, took the initiative to create events like Massacre Fest. Dedicated to metal, it began in 2011 and brought together Los Santos bands and nationally recognized acts. That same year, Gabo Montero and Luis Ricardo Castro, “Pizza,” founded Neurótica Producciones and began organizing many of the concerts held during that period.
“Tito Fest,” organized by Tito Picado, Gabo Montero, and friends (2011)

That generational handover and continuity may have made it easier to consider reviving the festival ten years later. The circumstances were encouraging: many of us were returning to the region after finishing university. There was greater maturity—
try not to fall over in surprise, eh!
—and knowledge to take on a project like the festival again. Once more, the convergence of people from the early-2000s scene and those who had followed them proved essential.

There is also an emotional element worth mentioning. It was 2016. I was walking from San Pedro de Montes de Oca toward Curridabat when it hit me: that year marked ten years since the first festival. Nostalgia got the better of me. When I got home, I created a WhatsApp group, added the friends I knew might be up for it, and named it Santos Rock 2016.
It is January 2017, and we are back

I think Pablo Zúñiga was the first to reply, with surprised emojis (“😱😱😱😱”). I realized everyone I had added was excited by the idea. We began figuring out how to put everything together again. Some decisions were unavoidable, starting with whether to return to El Guayabal. We agreed to do so. But the dates of the towns’ traditional year-end patron saint festivities pushed us to hold the festival in January instead of December, as we had for the first two editions. We had also begun working late in the year, so aiming for the first month of the next year gave us more time to get organized.

The organizing group grew over time. I wanted to bring in the experience of those who had remained more active in the Los Santos scene while many of my friends and I had stepped away. Gabriel Montero was one of those additions, since Neurótica Producciones had been organizing events, particularly metal shows. Cristopher Barboza joined too, bringing experience with punk concerts. Many friends who had played in bands at the first Santos Rock festivals, participating more as musicians than organizers, now took on logistical tasks, including Pablo Zúñiga, Frin Durán, and “Josa” Porras.

Our combined contacts made it easier to build the lineup and hire sound, lighting, security, and the thousand other things these events always require. We started making noise as soon as we could, and excitement kept growing. Cris Barboza passed that enthusiasm on to his dad, and we soon added Anestesia Local to the lineup: the pioneering band that began playing rock in Tarrazú in the 1990s, with Luis Barboza, “Popocho”—Cris’s dad—singing alongside Canadian Bruce Callow.

Another example of generations coming together was Gargamel’s reunion. This pioneering band began playing punk in Tarrazú in the early 2000s. Two members, Fabián and Maikol Mora, had died in a tragic traffic accident descending the Abejonal in May 2006. Now, more than ten years later, Gargamel returned to the stage with Cris on drums and Pil on guitar: two members of PuerkoXpin, the punk band formed in 2011 and Gargamel’s undisputed successor.
Gargamel at Santos Rock 2017
We keep dancing, dreaming, singing (
as Santo Remedio says

That meeting of generations, which defined Santos Rock’s return, was fundamental. I would also say it has been the secret behind the festival’s continuity ever since. When preparations began for the edition following 2017, I decided to step aside and focus on my academic commitments. When I attended the January 2018 festival with friends from San José, I became convinced of something: I had conceived an idea, but it could continue perfectly well without me. The 2018 festival was excellent. My friends had secured a better stage, planned a lineup balanced across musical genres, delivered impeccable sound, and drawn a strong crowd
Seka at Santos Rock 2018

Although I rejoined the organizers the following year, I did so simply to help facilitate things. Besides organizing another festival, we tried to realize some earlier aspirations. We introduced a more professional graphic style and visual identity. We secured a Declaration of Cultural Interest from the Ministry of Culture and Youth, expanded media coverage, and obtained a good number of sponsors and institutional supporters. A documentary was filmed, briefly reviewing previous editions and taking stock of what had been achieved by 2019. We also established the Santos Rock Cultural Association, whose founding statutes identified its main purpose as “supporting, promoting, publicizing, and accompanying alternative artistic expressions arising in the particular context of the Los Santos region, especially musical initiatives related to rock and similar genres.”

In the middle of that year, I moved to Mexico City to study and live, building a life far removed from the Los Santos music scene that I care about so much. For that reason, I do not feel able to continue a first-person, openly testimonial account of a process in which I have not been directly involved. I would, however, like to consider how that distance allows me to address something relevant to understanding what continues to happen in the scene generally and at Santos Rock specifically.

The formation, development, and consolidation of a music scene depend on more than musicians, bands, and places to gather, drink beer, and make noise. They also need management, organization, and leadership. A scene can only endure and reinvent itself, however, when people hand over responsibility and leadership does not become entrenched. I can say confidently that this openness and reinvention have benefited Los Santos’ music scene. This may have led some people to distance themselves critically, which is entirely understandable and valid, especially when they feel that the way the festival is organized and its annual lineup have moved away from an ideal or from what worked before.

Beyond that nuance, it is worth observing how the cultural association, established in mid-2019 and now responsible for organizing the festival and other cultural events, has gained momentum and fresh energy through changes in leadership and the continual arrival of new members. That keeps the festival, and the wider scene, from becoming merely an anecdote. I would like to recognize and thank everyone involved in the association for their committed, professional work, particularly Jéssica and Javi, who have served as its presidents over these years.
Cris Barboza, Shirley Montero, and their daughter Alina at Santos Rock (2020)

That, I believe, is the main reason to celebrate twenty years of the idea and dream we had as kids pasting posters on utility poles. The first festival, born amid difficulties but with enormous enthusiasm, had a very clear goal. That idea remains the same today. It is also the glue joining the dedication, commitment, and spirit of the young people who now take our place.

The idea is that our friends’ and neighbors’ music has value, deserves to be shared in the best possible way, and has every merit needed to reach stages within and beyond our country. As long as people want to keep making noise, writing irreverent lyrics, gathering to start a
mosh pit
and celebrating friendship, that idea will remain alive.
Jesús Bedoya Ureña
Mexico City, Friday, October 10, 2025.

I thank Erandi Barroso for her attentive reading and valuable editorial comments. My thanks also go to Marco Méndez and Javier Solís for their observations, and to Pablo Zúñiga, Gabriel Montero, Álex Jiménez, and Cristopher Barboza for the information they provided.
